turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, doctor. Well, I'm here because... I just keep blowing up at people over nothing. It's, uh, it's getting really bad. I'm snapping at my team on operations calls at work, and... and even at my family when I get home. That is just not how I've ever handled things. I've always been pretty level-headed, so... yeah, I don't really know what's going on with me, but I need to get it under control.

symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient describes frequent angry outbursts and verbal aggression with little provocation, specifically blowing up at people over nothing and snapping at coworkers and family.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start noticing this change in your temper? Was it something that started recently, or has this been going on for a while?
turns.patient_response: It's been going on for about three weeks now. It started right after we had a valve failure at the facility. There was an injury when it happened, and... yeah, ever since that day, my temper has just been completely out of control.

symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient explicitly confirms that their temper has been completely out of control following a traumatic valve failure and injury at work three weeks ago, consistent with trauma-related irritable behavior and angry outbursts.

turns.doctor_question: Besides the irritability, have you noticed any changes in your mood over these past three weeks—like feeling sad, down, or anxious?
turns.patient_response:
I wouldn't really say I feel sad or anxious, exactly. It's more like... I just can't feel good about anything right now. 

My wife will make dinner, or my kids will talk about soccer like normal, and I know I should feel glad to be there with them. But... I don't know, it’s like there’s nothing in me that can respond. I just can't feel happy about it.

symptom_reasoning.S076: The patient describes an inability to experience positive emotions, stating they cannot feel good or happy even when spending time with their family.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient denies feeling sad when asked about changes in mood.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient denies feeling anxious when asked about mood changes.

turns.doctor_question: When you say you can't feel happy about things—did that feeling of numbness start right away on the day of the valve failure, or did it develop gradually over those three weeks?
turns.patient_response: I'm not exactly sure when it started, to be honest. It's hard to pinpoint a specific day. I just know that over the last few weeks, it's become really obvious to me that I'm just... not feeling anything positive. I don't know if it hit me all at once that day or if it just kind of crept up on me, but it's definitely been there since the accident.

symptom_reasoning.S076: The patient explicitly confirms an ongoing inability to feel positive emotions, stating that over the last few weeks they are 'not feeling anything positive.'

turns.doctor_question: Before this valve failure three weeks ago, have you ever experienced periods in your life where you felt depressed, numb, or had these kinds of mood problems lasting days or weeks?
turns.patient_response: No, never. I've never had anything like this happen before. I mean, sure, everyone gets stressed or has a bad day, but... not like this. I've never had a time where I just couldn't feel anything good for weeks on end. This is all completely new to me, and it definitely only started after the accident at the facility.

turns.doctor_question: Since the accident at the facility, have you been having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about what happened that day?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I have. I can just be sitting at the kitchen table, or... or trying to answer some emails from home, and suddenly I'm right back there. I just see the flash from that valve and the smoke in the aisle. It's like it just... shoves everything else right out of my head.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient reports experiencing intrusive, sudden recollections and vivid flashbacks of the traumatic accident while engaged in everyday activities.

turns.doctor_question: Besides these flashbacks that pop up on their own, have you been deliberately trying to stay away from things that remind you of the accident—like avoiding certain areas of the facility, or certain people, or even talking about what happened?
turns.patient_response: I don't think so, no. I mean, I haven't been back to work since it happened, so I guess I haven't really had to face being near that aisle or anything. But I haven't been actively trying to avoid people from work or changing the subject if someone brings it up. It's just... I'm mostly at home right now anyway, so it hasn't really come up like that.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly denies actively avoiding people from work, changing the subject, or deliberately staying away from reminders of the accident.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed yourself avoiding things at home—like certain TV shows, conversations, or activities—because they might remind you of the accident or make you feel the way you do now?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I mean, I watch TV and talk to my wife just like normal. I haven't been avoiding any specific shows or anything like that. I'm just... sitting around the house a lot. But I'm not actively trying to avoid anything at home.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly denies avoiding reminders, conversations, or television shows related to the accident at home.

turns.doctor_question: Since the accident, have you found yourself thinking things like 'I should have prevented this' or 'I can't be trusted to do my job safely,' or has your general view of how safe the world is changed?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think I've had thoughts like that. I know accidents happen in this line of work, and... well, I was just doing my job the way I always do. I haven't really been blaming myself or thinking I can't do my job. And I don't feel like the whole world is unsafe now or anything. It's just... that specific thing that happened, it just keeps coming back to me. But no, I haven't been beating myself up over it or thinking everything is dangerous now.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient states that the specific event 'just keeps coming back to me,' indicating recurrent, intrusive memories of the accident.
symptom_reasoning.S072: The patient explicitly denies developing negative beliefs about their capability or believing that the world is unsafe or dangerous.
symptom_reasoning.S073: The patient explicitly denies self-blame or feeling responsible for the accident, stating they have not been blaming or beating themselves up.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been avoiding going back to work or making excuses not to return to the facility since the accident?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't been making excuses or avoiding it. I'm just out on medical leave right now because of my injuries. The doctor said I needed time to heal up before I could go back. So it's not like I'm choosing to stay away or trying to get out of it... I'm just following orders until I'm cleared to work again.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly denies avoiding returning to work or making excuses to stay away from the facility following the accident, stating they are simply on medical leave.

turns.doctor_question: Since the accident, have you noticed changes in your sleep—like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or being on high alert even when you're trying to rest?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, my sleep has been pretty terrible. Most nights I just lie there in bed, and I keep hearing that alarm going off in my head. It makes it really hard to wind down. And then, when I finally do manage to doze off, it doesn't last. I keep waking up sweating from these dreams about the smoke, and hearing people yelling... so by the time morning rolls around, I feel like I never slept at all.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient reports severe difficulty falling asleep, broken sleep, waking up sweating from nightmares, and non-restorative rest.
symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient reports recurrent, distressing trauma-related dreams involving smoke and people yelling from the accident.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
